content: Carbon black is a material typically produced through the incomplete combustion of petroleum products. It is a form of amorphous carbon characterized by an extremely high surface area-to-volume ratio, making it one of the earliest nanomaterials to be widely utilized. While it is similar to soot, carbon black has a significantly higher surface area-to-volume ratio. It is commonly used as a pigment and as a reinforcing agent in rubber and plastic products. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) currently classifies carbon black as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). Short-term exposure to high concentrations of carbon black dust can cause discomfort in the upper respiratory tract due to mechanical irritation. The most prevalent application of carbon black is as a pigment and reinforcing phase in automobile tires. It also aids in dissipating heat from the tread and belt areas of tires, thereby reducing thermal damage and extending tire lifespan. Additionally, carbon black particles are used in radar-absorbing materials and printer toner. Approximately 1 million tonnes of carbon black were produced in 2006, with about 20% of global production allocated to belts, hoses, and other rubber goods. The remaining production is used in inks and as a pigment for non-tire products. Carbon black derived from vegetable sources is used as a food coloring agent, known in Europe as additive E153. The primary use of carbon black is as a reinforcing filler in rubber products, particularly in tires. For example, rubber without carbon black has a tensile strength of about 5 MPa and negligible abrasion resistance. However, compounding rubber with 50% of its weight in carbon black significantly improves its tensile strength and wear resistance. Nearly all rubber products requiring high tensile strength and abrasion resistance utilize carbon black, which is why they are black in color. In cases where physical properties are important but non-black colors are desired, such as in white tennis shoes, precipitated or fumed silica serves as a viable alternative to carbon black for reinforcement. Silica-based fillers are also gaining market share in automotive tires due to their superior fuel efficiency, attributed to lower rolling losses compared to carbon black-filled tires. Although silica fillers traditionally had inferior abrasion resistance, advancements in technology have improved their performance to match that of carbon black. Carbon black, also known as Pigment Black (Colour Index International, PBL-7), is a common black pigment historically produced by charring organic materials such as wood or bone. It consists of pure elemental carbon and appears black because it reflects almost no light in the visible spectrum. It has been known by various names, each reflecting traditional production methods. For instance, ivory black was made by charring ivory or animal bones, vine black was produced by charring desiccated grape vines and stems, and lamp black was obtained by collecting soot from oil lamps. Modern production methods have largely replaced these traditional techniques, although some materials are still produced using these methods for artisanal purposes. Carbon black particles may have surface oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carboxylic, quinonic, lactonic, phenolic groups) to varying degrees depending on manufacturing conditions. These surface oxygen groups are collectively referred to as volatile content. Due to this volatile content, carbon black is considered a non-conductive material. In the coatings and inks industries, acid-oxidized grades of carbon black are preferred. During manufacturing, acid is sprayed in high-temperature dryers to alter the inherent surface chemistry of the carbon black. This process increases the amount of chemically bonded oxygen on the surface area of the carbon black, thereby enhancing its performance characteristics.
